observation: KYC is the largest single leak in the onboarding funnel.
evidence: 70.5% of mature registrants complete KYC; 2,687 of 6,308 users lost across all stages (42.6%). Median time to KYC is 6 days (p75 9).
implication: Fixing KYC has more headroom than any other stage because it sits at the top and compounds through every later stage.
recommendation: Run EXP-01 (guided KYC + reminders) and EXP-02 (assisted KYC for stalled applicants).
label: ACTUAL

observation: Users who contact support while a stage is pending are far less likely to complete it.
evidence: KYC completion: 7.5% for ticket raisers vs 74.9% for non-raisers; deposit 27.1% vs 78.9%. Only 6.5% of at-risk users raised a related ticket.
implication: A ticket is a visible signal of a blocked user. Association only (blocked users raise tickets); it does not prove that tickets cause drop-off.
recommendation: Prioritise first-contact resolution on onboarding tickets; trigger a proactive follow-up for open onboarding tickets older than 24h.
kpi: Stage completion within 14 days of an onboarding ticket
label: ACTUAL (association)

observation: First deposit is the second-largest bottleneck, and deposit-to-trade is the third.
evidence: Bank->deposit 76.9% (1,305 lost); deposit->trade 79.8% (878 lost). Registered->first trade is 38.0%; registered->30-day active is 30.8%.
implication: Even after the bank is linked, about 1 in 4 users never funds the account, and about 1 in 5 funded users never trades.
recommendation: Run EXP-04 (low-ticket deposit prompt) and EXP-05 (guided first trade with practice order).
label: ACTUAL

observation: Time from registration to first trade is long relative to the stage lags.
evidence: Median registration->first trade is 23 days (p75 28); stage medians KYC 6d, bank 4d, deposit 7d, trade 6d. Channel spread in timing is only about 2 days.
implication: Lag is spread across all four steps rather than concentrated in one; no channel is materially faster, so onboarding speed is a product issue, not a channel issue.
recommendation: Add day-based reminders at each stage; track time-to-first-trade as an onboarding KPI.
label: ACTUAL

observation: Referral and organic channels deliver the highest-quality users; paid social and partnerships the lowest.
evidence: First-trade rate (mature): Referral 52.9%, Organic 47.2%, Paid Search 36.6%, Paid Social 30.3%, Partnerships 31.1%. Channel differences are significant (chi-square p<0.001).
implication: Registration volume and quality are decoupled: paid social is 25% of registrations but has the lowest first-trade rate among the large channels.
recommendation: Judge channels on cost per first trader, not CAC alone.
kpi: Cost per first trader at maturity, by channel
label: ACTUAL

observation: Organic traffic is only a minority of registrations but is the best-performing large source.
evidence: Organic is 18.8% of registrations; first-trade rate 47.2% vs 35.8% for paid/incentivised; 30-day active 62.7% vs 52.0% (p<0.001).
implication: Organic cannot be bought with budget, but its quality sets a benchmark; no CAC is recorded for it (shown as not defined, not zero).
recommendation: Invest in organic search/social content and referral loops; track organic spend separately if content costs are available.
kpi: Organic share of registrations; organic first-trade rate
label: ACTUAL

observation: Customer Referral (CMP05) is the most cost-efficient campaign; Video Awareness (CMP04) and Finance Affiliate (CMP06) are the least.
evidence: Cost per first trader at maturity: CMP05 Rs 438 (CI Rs 413-Rs 466); CMP04 Rs 1,252; CMP06 Rs 1,216. CMP04 first-trade rate is significantly below the rest (Holm p<0.001); CMP06 is not significant after correction (p=0.061) although its cost per trader is high.
implication: CMP05 and CMP04/CMP06 sit at opposite ends of the scorecard; CMP06 needs more data before a firm conclusion. CI reflects conversion-rate uncertainty only (CAC treated as fixed).
recommendation: Scale CMP05 within its capacity; put CMP04 and CMP06 on a performance improvement plan.
kpi: Cost per first trader at maturity
label: ACTUAL (scorecard is analyst-defined, not a model)

observation: Moving budget from the two weakest to the two strongest paid campaigns is arithmetically attractive but highly sensitive to diminishing returns.
evidence: Scenario: move 25% of CMP04 and CMP06 budgets (Rs 190,000) to CMP05 and CMP10. At observed efficiency the net gain is about 265 first traders (9.1% of the paid baseline); it falls to 55 if destination costs double and reaches break-even only when destination cost per first trader is about +172% above observed.
implication: Not a forecast: referral and CRM have limited absorptive capacity, so incremental spend will likely cost more than the average.
recommendation: Stage the shift (10%, then 25%) and re-measure marginal cost per first trader at each step.
kpi: Marginal cost per first trader by campaign
label: SCENARIO (arithmetic, not forecast)

observation: Retention decays steadily rather than collapsing after onboarding.
evidence: Calendar-month retention (mature cohorts): M1 67.6%, M3 56.0%, M6 40.7%. 30-day active 54.0% of eligible; 90-day inactivity proxy 14.9%; 22.0% dormant for the last 3 months.
implication: About 12 points of retention are lost between M1 and M3 and a further 15 points by M6, so the retention plan must start in months 1-3.
recommendation: Run EXP-07 (habit nudges) and build a month-1 engagement milestone into onboarding.
kpi: M1, M3, M6 retention; dormant-3m rate
label: ACTUAL (inactivity PROXIES, not churn)

observation: Referral and organic cohorts retain best; partnerships and affiliate retain worst.
evidence: M3 retention: Referral 61.2%, Organic 60.4%, Partnerships 50.8%, Paid Social 54.1%. 3-month dormancy: Referral 15.5% vs Affiliate 25.2%. Channel M3 differences significant (p<0.001).
implication: The channels that acquire cheaply are not the ones that keep customers.
recommendation: Include M3 retention in the campaign scorecard (already done) and review quarterly.
label: ACTUAL

observation: Early trading is associated with better later retention, but early signals are weak predictors.
evidence: M3 retained 60.7% when traded in months 0-1 vs 50.0% when not. A logistic early-warning prototype has CV AUC 0.57 (temporal test 0.58).
implication: Activation timing matters, but the available features cannot reliably predict who will disengage; this is an association and not a causal estimate.
recommendation: Focus on universal onboarding improvements, not on risk-score targeting, until richer behavioural data exist.
kpi: Share of new users trading in months 0-1
label: ACTUAL (association; model weak)

observation: A large share of customers are stalled in onboarding rather than inactive after trading.
evidence: Journey segments: KYC-pending 28.3%, deposit-pending 13.3%, bank-link pending 8.2%, deposited-never-traded 8.8%; high-engagement traders are only 9.0% and repeat traders 16.8%. K-means (k=4, silhouette 0.33) shows continuous, weakly separated clusters.
implication: By the funnel flags, 58.6% of users sit in a stalled onboarding state. The high source-conflict share in those segments (91-98%) means many also appear active in the activity log, so the true size of the backlog is uncertain.
recommendation: Reconcile funnel flags with activity data before targeting; run stage-specific nudges for 'stalled' users.
kpi: Share of mature users in stalled segments
label: ACTUAL (conflict-flagged)

observation: Support volume is high and concentrated in onboarding and trading categories.
evidence: 7,614 tickets (761 per 1,000 users; 52% of users raised at least one). KYC 22.7% of tickets (26.7 per 1,000 customer-months), trading & orders 17.2%. Median resolution 9.4h; CSAT 3.83; 892 open and 479 escalated.
implication: Onboarding-related tickets (KYC, bank, deposit) together account for over half of all tickets, so product fixes should reduce volume more efficiently than staffing.
recommendation: Run EXP-08; add in-flow help to KYC and bank-link screens.
kpi: Tickets per 1,000 customer-months; onboarding ticket share
label: ACTUAL

observation: Priority does not change service levels, and the backlog is ageing.
evidence: Median resolution is about 9.4-9.5h for High, Medium and Low priority alike (Kruskal-Wallis p=0.59); CSAT vs resolution time correlation 0.02. 563 unresolved tickets are older than 90 days, 208 older than 180 days.
implication: The priority field appears not to drive routing in this synthetic data, and old open tickets are unmanaged risk. Real operations may differ.
recommendation: Introduce SLA tiers by priority and a weekly backlog clearance for tickets older than 90 days.
kpi: Resolution time by priority; open tickets >90 days
label: ACTUAL

observation: Support contact is only weakly associated with later inactivity.
evidence: Cohort-adjusted odds ratio of 3-month dormancy for users who raised any ticket: 1.15 (95% CI 1.03-1.30); raising 3+ tickets: borderline (CI crosses 1). CSAT does not separate dormancy (23-24% across CSAT bands).
implication: Support experience is not a strong standalone driver of inactivity here; do not over-invest on that basis alone. Association, not causation.
recommendation: Keep support improvements justified by onboarding conversion and cost-to-serve rather than by a retention claim.
label: ACTUAL (weak association)
